chapter: The Original Dixieland band to California
title: Joining the union and the transfer card rule
summary: The band joined the union in Houston, but San Francisco required transfer cards and ten percent of earnings.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: You were asking about the union before. Well, before we left Houston, Texas, we joined the union.
Was it the international union, or....?
Yeah, this was the regular Musicians Union. But none of us had ever belonged to a union before.

We joined because we knew when we got to California... Hill and them knew you had to be in the union to play in a lot of these places. Because this guy Hill owned a cigar factory. See? And they knew that much, that if you didn't belong to the union, you wasn't gonna get any job, especially on that radio station or in this restaurant in San Francisco.
Why was California so organized with the unions and all that, and none of the other states were?

Well, the big cities was. Houston was... Texas had it. I think New Orleans had a union. But I don't think many of the Black people belonged to it. And during that time, they had a law. When you went into a jurisdiction, you had to put in what you call a transfer card. You see?
That carried on just until a little while ago, didn't it?
Yeah. Well, they've kind of stopped that. Then you had to pay 10 percent of your earnings...!
That's right. In San Francisco. San Francisco was the toughest union town on musicians in the United States
